ste.about: Vary flow rates and inlet temperatures across a two-pass exchanger, then derive the effectiveness–NTU relationship from your own readings.
outcomes: Determine log mean temperature difference from measured inlet and outlet conditions
Compare countercurrent and cocurrent arrangements at matched duty

v.t: What does the effectiveness (ε) of a heat exchanger compare?
opts: The actual heat transfer with the largest heat transfer possible
The hot-side flow rate with the cold-side flow rate
The overall heat transfer coefficient with the surface area
The hot fluid’s inlet temperature with its outlet temperature
v.expl: ε = q ÷ q_max, where q_max = C_min (T_h,in − T_c,in).

v.t: How is the number of transfer units (NTU) defined?
opts: UA ÷ C_min
C_min ÷ C_max
q ÷ q_max
UA ÷ C_max
v.expl: NTU = UA ÷ C_min — the exchanger’s size measured against the smaller heat-capacity rate.

v.t: In a counter-flow exchanger, what can happen that cannot happen in parallel flow?
opts: The cold fluid can leave hotter than the hot fluid leaves
The hot fluid can leave colder than the cold fluid enters
Both fluids can leave at their inlet temperatures
The heat duty can exceed C_min (T_h,in − T_c,in)
v.expl: In counter flow the cold fluid meets the hottest hot fluid near its exit, so its outlet can rise above the hot outlet.

v.t: Fouling on the tube surfaces lowers the overall heat transfer coefficient U.
v.expl: Fouling adds a thermal resistance in series, so U falls.

v.t: For the same inlet conditions and UA, parallel flow transfers more heat than counter flow.
v.expl: Counter flow keeps a larger mean temperature difference, so it transfers more heat for the same UA.

v.t: Explain how fouling changes the exchanger’s performance, using what you observed in the simulation.
v.guide: Look for: fouling adds a thermal resistance; U falls; at the same flow rates the heat duty and the effectiveness fall; the outlet temperatures move towards their inlet values. Give credit for linking this to readings taken in the simulation, and for mentioning cleaning or a fouling allowance in design.
v.expl: Fouling adds a resistance, so U and the heat duty fall at the same flow rates: the hot fluid leaves hotter and the cold fluid leaves cooler.

q.t: What is the log mean temperature difference (LMTD) used for?
opts: Sizing an exchanger from Q = U·A·ΔT_lm
Measuring the fouling resistance directly
Setting the pump flow rate
Converting effectiveness into NTU
q.expl: Q = U·A·ΔT_lm links the heat duty, the area and the temperature difference.

q.t: Counter flow always needs a larger area than parallel flow for the same duty.
q.expl: Counter flow needs less area for the same duty because its mean temperature difference is larger.

q.t: Compare countercurrent and cocurrent arrangements at matched duty, using your readings.
q.guide: Look for: counter flow gives the larger LMTD and needs less area for the same duty; readings from both arrangements are quoted; the temperature cross that only counter flow allows is mentioned.
q.expl: Counter flow gives the larger mean temperature difference, so it needs less area for the same duty.

asms.name: Heat Exchanger — post-lab
asms.intro: Four short questions on what you measured in the Shell-and-Tube Heat Exchanger simulation. One answer is written; your faculty marks it.

ans.Q-0106: In the WEB run I turned the fouling up and kept both flow rates the same. The hot fluid left hotter than before and the cold fluid left cooler, so less heat was passed across. Fouling is an extra layer of resistance, so U goes down and the effectiveness goes down with it. That is why exchangers are cleaned, or designed with extra area.
Fouling builds up on the tubes and acts like insulation. The overall coefficient U drops, so for the same flows the exchanger transfers less heat and both outlet temperatures change less.

sc.t: Which fluid sets C_min in the effectiveness–NTU method?
opts: The fluid with the smaller heat-capacity rate, ṁc_p
The fluid with the higher inlet temperature
The fluid on the shell side
The fluid with the larger mass flow rate
sc.expl: C_min is the smaller of the two heat-capacity rates (ṁc_p), whichever side that fluid is on.

sc.t: At a fixed capacity ratio, what happens to the effectiveness as NTU increases?
opts: It rises and levels off
It falls
It stays the same
It rises without limit
sc.expl: More transfer units means more area for the same C_min, so ε rises towards its limit.

sc.t: Why is a correction factor F applied to the LMTD of a two-pass shell-and-tube exchanger?
opts: Its flow is neither pure counter flow nor pure parallel flow
The two fluids have different densities
The tubes conduct heat along their length
The shell loses heat to the room
sc.expl: Multi-pass flow mixes counter-flow and parallel-flow sections, so the counter-flow LMTD is multiplied by F ≤ 1.

sc.t: What does the capacity ratio C_r compare?
opts: C_min with C_max
U with A
q with q_max
The inlet temperature with the outlet temperature
sc.expl: C_r = C_min ÷ C_max, so it lies between 0 and 1.

sc.t: Which change raises the heat duty at the same inlet temperatures and flow rates?
opts: Increasing the heat transfer area
Letting fouling build up on the tubes
Switching from counter flow to parallel flow
Shortening the tubes
sc.expl: More area raises UA and NTU, so more heat is transferred.

tf.t: When one fluid condenses at constant temperature, the capacity ratio C_r is effectively zero.
tf.expl: A condensing fluid behaves like one with a very large heat-capacity rate, so C_min ÷ C_max approaches zero.

tf.t: The LMTD is always larger than the arithmetic mean of the two end temperature differences.
tf.expl: The LMTD is smaller than or equal to the arithmetic mean; they are equal only when the two end differences are equal.

tf.t: Raising the cold-side flow rate, with everything else unchanged, lowers the cold outlet temperature.
tf.expl: With more flow, each kilogram of cold fluid picks up less heat, so its outlet temperature falls.

tf.t: Designers usually allow for fouling by adding a fouling resistance when they calculate U.
tf.expl: A fouling factor is added to the thermal resistances, which lowers the design U.

tf.t: In parallel flow, the cold fluid can leave hotter than the hot fluid leaves.
tf.expl: Only counter flow allows this temperature cross; in parallel flow both outlets approach a common temperature.

w.t: Using your readings, explain how changing the hot-side flow rate affected the effectiveness.
w.guide: Look for: readings at two or more hot-side flow rates; the effect on C_hot, C_min and NTU; a conclusion about the effectiveness that follows from the readings.
w.expl: If the hot fluid sets C_min, a higher hot-side flow raises C_min and lowers NTU, so the effectiveness falls even though the duty may rise.

w.t: Describe how you found the log mean temperature difference from your measured temperatures.
w.guide: Look for: the four terminal temperatures; the two end differences for the arrangement used; the LMTD formula applied correctly; units.
w.expl: ΔT_lm = (ΔT_1 − ΔT_2) ÷ ln(ΔT_1 ÷ ΔT_2), using the end differences for the flow arrangement.

w.t: Explain why counter flow can give a temperature cross, using your simulation results.
w.guide: Look for: what a temperature cross is; readings where the cold outlet is above the hot outlet; why parallel flow cannot do this.
w.expl: In counter flow the cold fluid leaves next to the hot inlet, so it can be heated above the hot outlet temperature.

w.t: Suggest one change that would raise the exchanger’s duty, and justify it with the ε–NTU relationship.
w.guide: Look for: a concrete change such as more area, a higher U or counter flow; its effect on NTU or C_r; the resulting change in effectiveness and duty.
w.expl: For example, more area raises NTU, which raises ε and so the duty q = ε C_min (T_h,in − T_c,in).

w.t: Compare the duty you measured with the duty the ε–NTU method predicts, and explain any difference.
w.guide: Look for: both values with units; the size of the difference; reasons such as heat loss, reading error or fouling.
w.expl: Differences usually come from heat lost to the surroundings, reading error, or fouling the prediction left out.
